references_named: Walter Benjamin, The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction (1935)
rationale: A disciplined digital readymade of Brouwn's distance works: the pointer replaces the foot, the CSS reference pixel supplies a fake-but-declared conversion, and the path is refused exactly as Brouwn refused it. The mechanism is the concept (P1) — the page cannot be a print, cannot be screenshotted into the work, and forgets on close. The Brouwn/browser pun and the dry footer copy carry the cheerful-cynic voice well, and the restraint (one number, one step count, no path, no persistence) is exemplary of P3. Narrative placement in the twenty-year argument is coherent: a fresh web-native embodiment of a canonical gesture, sitting on the chance/order axis.
reservations: The Benjamin framing is asserted in the motivation more than enacted in the work itself. The piece reads as a clean Brouwn digital readymade; the reproduction-problem gloss sits on top rather than being dramatized. The 750mm step length is a touch arbitrary (acknowledged as 'Brouwn's own foot withheld') — defensible but slightly soft. The work also risks slight category overlap with The Unkept and 1000 Hours of Staring in using browser attention/presence as material, though the mechanism and source are clearly distinct.
revision_suggestion: Either dramatize the Benjamin dimension inside the page (e.g., a single line of running text noting that the number, unlike the path, is exactly reproducible — 'the work and its copy are the same number, which is the problem') or drop Benjamin from the references and let the piece stand cleanly as a Brouwn digital readymade. The current dual citation slightly dilutes the otherwise surgical focus.
